module_title: Advanced Analysis - Panch Prayag, Border Nomenclature, and Distributaries
introduction: This advanced level provides a microscopic look at the formation of the Ganga in Uttarakhand (the Five Prayags), how river names change drastically as they cross international borders, and the mechanics of delta formation.

core_concepts.title: Panch Prayag (The Five Confluences)
core_concepts.description: In Uttarakhand, the confluences of the Alaknanda river with other rivers are called Prayags: 1. Vishnuprayag (Dhauliganga + Alaknanda), 2. Nandprayag (Nandakini + Alaknanda), 3. Karnaprayag (Pindar + Alaknanda), 4. Rudraprayag (Mandakini + Alaknanda), 5. Devprayag (Bhagirathi + Alaknanda). Only after Devprayag is the river officially called 'Ganga'.

core_concepts.title: Nomenclature of Brahmaputra
core_concepts.description: In Tibet = Tsangpo; Upon entering Arunachal Pradesh = Dihang; In the Assam Valley = Brahmaputra; Upon entering Bangladesh = Jamuna.

core_concepts.title: Nomenclature of Ganga and the Meghna System
core_concepts.description: When the Ganga enters Bangladesh, it is called the 'Padma'. When the Padma (Ganga) and the Jamuna (Brahmaputra) merge, the combined stream is still called the Padma. Further downstream, when the 'Barak/Meghna' river joins it, the massive combined river finally empties into the Bay of Bengal as the 'Meghna'.

core_concepts.title: The Hooghly Distributary
core_concepts.description: At Farakka in West Bengal, the Ganga bifurcates (splits) into two streams: the main branch continues into Bangladesh as the Padma, while the other branch flows south through Kolkata as the Bhagirathi-Hooghly. The Hooghly is a 'Distributary', not a tributary.

important_entities.name: Barak River
important_entities.significance: Originating in the Manipur hills, this river becomes a crucial part of the Ganga-Brahmaputra basin in Bangladesh. It is the river that ultimately gives the 'Meghna' its name before hitting the ocean.

trap_alerts_and_exceptions.explanation: The Yamuna is a 'Tributary' of the Ganga (it adds water to the Ganga). The Hooghly is a 'Distributary' of the Ganga (it takes water away from the Ganga and flows independently to the sea).
Students frequently confuse the confluences of the Mandakini and the Bhagirathi. The Mandakini (coming from Kedarnath) meets at Rudraprayag. The Bhagirathi (coming from Gangotri) meets at Devprayag.

mnemonics_and_tricks.explanation:
B-Bhagirathi + A-Alaknanda = D-Devprayag. 
M-Mandakini + A-Alaknanda = R-Rudraprayag.

exam_strategy_tips: UPSC frequently asks for the correct North-to-South sequence of the Panch Prayag: Vishnu -> Nand -> Karna -> Rudra -> Dev.

In Assertion-Reasoning questions, note that the Brahmaputra (Tsangpo) carries less water and silt in Tibet because it is a cold, dry region. It is only after it enters India that heavy rainfall causes it to carry massive amounts of water and silt.
